source_reviews.independent_solution: A mechanical wave is a disturbance or oscillation propagating through an elastic medium by interactions between particles. Isolated periodic particle motion is not enough: the disturbance must propagate to other positions. This follows from n38 blocks 0, 5, 6 and 8.

coverage.evidence: n39-wave-basics A requires the propagation definition; B and D distinguish it from bulk particle transport and no motion. The merged item also requires source 3's local-motion/energy distinction in C. Unaided definition production is explicitly lost, not silently claimed.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Transverse particle motion is perpendicular to propagation, exemplified by a sideways wave on an elastic cord. Longitudinal motion is parallel to propagation, exemplified by along-chain-driven spring-connected balls with traveling compressions and rarefactions. Both the direction rules and both example assignments are required by the written task; n38 blocks 0, 5, 6 and 8 supply them.

coverage.evidence: n39-wave-types gives both definitions and both examples in every complete alternative. Correct direction rules alone leave A and D, so example matching remains necessary. Unaided comparison and example generation are recorded production losses; neither wave type is omitted.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The disturbance and mechanical energy propagate, while medium particles oscillate locally about equilibrium rather than traveling with the disturbance. Elastic coupling does work on successive neighbors. The outgoing model has finite successive response delays, not instantaneous onset everywhere; n38 blocks 5, 6 and 8 and n39 block 6 establish the local-motion model.

coverage.evidence: The combined n39-wave-basics item requires C as well as A and rejects material transport, permanent rest and simultaneous onset. Source 3 is not replaced by merely recalling the wave definition. Its independent verbal explanation is honestly listed as a loss.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Wavelength is the smallest positive separation along propagation between distinct equal-phase points. Equal phase includes the stage/direction of motion, not just coincident displacement. Figure 70 shows in-phase pairs 1-13, 2-14 and 3-15 and antiphase pair 1-7. An arbitrary equal-phase separation can be 2lambda, and the nearest antiphase separation is lambda/2.

coverage.evidence: n39-wavelength B retains nearest, distinct and same phase together. A tests loss of the nearest quantifier, C confuses amplitude and D confuses a half-cycle. The item loses unaided wording, not a defining condition.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The wave advances lambda in one period T, giving v=lambda/T=lambda*nu with nu=1/T. At fixed frequency v is proportional to wavelength; wavelength alone does not set speed when frequency is unspecified. The relation holds for transverse and longitudinal waves and is not the individual particle's oscillatory velocity.

coverage.evidence: n39-wave-speed A preserves the full period and frequency forms. It does not introduce an unstated fixed-medium speed-change claim. The omitted unaided statement/explanation is recorded; the physical identity is retained as one complete response.

mathematics.independent_solution: Frozen before keys: one period advances one wavelength, hence v=lambda/T=lambda*nu. option_checks.evidence: Dividing wavelength advanced by period elapsed gives lambda/T; nu=1/T makes lambda*nu the equivalent expression.
Reversing the distance/time quotient yields T/lambda=1/(lambda*nu), with time/length units, not speed.
Multiplying travel distance by duration yields lambda*T=lambda/nu with length*time units; speed divides by duration.
Assigning a wavelength to each outward/return half-cycle invents 2lambda advance per T. The actual pattern advances lambda, so this is twice v.
